source_note: Hiroki Sayama, Introduction to the Modeling and Analysis of Complex Systems, Open SUNY Textbooks, Milne Library, State University of New York at Geneseo, 2015 (ISBN 978-1-942341-09-3 ebook; Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0). The local file is the complete publisher PDF of the textbook, 19,619,055 bytes, sha256 920564f2a1314d8e7fdf049f81a7e0a7acc651a50117e7552ff531260410c11b. Extracted text is clean and complete (about 123k words across 19 chapters plus front matter), with occasional line-break hyphenation and page headers interleaved; all verbatim quotes were chosen inside single pages and proven contiguous in the extracted text file. No catalog or title corrections needed. Motif-lane extraction (MOTIF-TIERB-DRAIN-01) of the same work for sync-cloud reconciliation.

primitives.name: A complex system is many microscopic components interacting in nontrivial ways, with key information in the relationships between parts
primitives.verbatim_quote: Complex systems are systems made of a large number of microscopic components interacting with each other in nontrivial ways.
primitives.page: About the Textbook, p. iii (text lines 45-47)
assumptions: The system has many components, not a handful
Interactions between components are nontrivial, i.e. not simple aggregation
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails as a working definition when component count is small or interactions are linear and separable, where reduction to parts is exact

layer2.mapping: A game, a league, or a roster is treated as a system whose output is carried by interactions among components rather than by component averages; the engine state must therefore include interaction terms, not only per-unit ratings.
layer2.telemetry: Per-component event streams plus pairwise interaction records (matchup snaps, shared minutes, coverage assignments)

primitives.name: Emergence is a nontrivial relationship between a system's properties at microscopic and macroscopic scales (Bar-Yam's definition, adopted by Sayama)
primitives.verbatim_quote: More concisely, emergence is a nontrivial relationship between the system’s properties at different scales.
assumptions: Properties are compared across at least two scales of description
The macro property is not the natural expectation from micro rules alone
primitives.breakdown_regime: The label is often applied loosely; without an explicit micro rule set and a macro observable, an emergence claim is untestable

layer2.mapping: Team-level outcomes (drive success, red zone conversion) are modeled as macro observables that need not equal sums of player grades; the reasoning layer checks whether a macro pattern is actually implied by the micro inputs before crediting it.
layer2.telemetry: Play-by-play micro events aggregated to drive, quarter, and game level outcomes for cross-scale comparison

primitives.name: Self-organization is a dynamical process in which an open system spontaneously produces macroscopic order over time
primitives.verbatim_quote: In other words, self-organization is a dynamical process that looks as if it were going against the second law of thermodynamics (which states that entropy of a closed system increases monotonically over time).
assumptions: The system is open, driven by energy or information flow from outside
Order arises from internal interactions, not from an external controller
primitives.breakdown_regime: Closed systems cannot self-organize in this sense; apparent order imposed by an external schedule or script is not self-organization

layer2.mapping: In-game momentum-like structure is only credited when it emerges from the play sequence itself (success breeding play-calling tendencies, fatigue accumulation), never inserted as an external narrative prior.
layer2.telemetry: Within-game play sequences, substitution patterns, and tempo series that could show spontaneous ordering

primitives.name: A model is a simplified representation of a system, and modeling is the only rational approach to an unreachable reality
primitives.verbatim_quote: A model is a simplified representation of a system. It can be conceptual, verbal, diagrammatic, physical, or formal (mathematical).
assumptions: Simplification is deliberate: some features of the real system are intentionally omitted
The representation must still answer the question it was built for
primitives.breakdown_regime: A model that reproduces the system in full detail is no longer a model; over-simplified models answer the wrong question precisely

layer2.mapping: Every engine projection is a representation with named omissions; the reasoning trail must state what the representation leaves out (for example unmodeled coaching adjustments) so confidence is priced against the simplification.
layer2.telemetry: Model registry entries listing included and excluded factors per projection type

primitives.name: A dynamical system is a system whose state is uniquely specified by a set of variables and whose behavior is described by predefined rules
primitives.verbatim_quote: A dynamical system is a system whose state is uniquely specified by a set of variables and whose behavior is described by predefined rules.
assumptions: The state variables suffice to specify the system at an instant
Rules are fixed in advance of the evolution being studied
primitives.breakdown_regime: If the rules themselves change with unmodeled context, the fixed-rule description breaks and the model must be re-specified

layer2.mapping: A matchup is encoded as a state vector (personnel, health, usage, situation) advanced by explicit transition rules (play outcomes, clock, field position), which is exactly the pre-play expectation and post-play grading loop the engine runs.
layer2.telemetry: State snapshots per play: down, distance, field position, personnel, score, clock, fatigue proxies

primitives.name: The phase space maps every state of a system to a unique spatial location, with one axis per degree of freedom
primitives.verbatim_quote: A phase space of a dynamical system is a theoretical space where every state of the system is mapped to a unique spatial location.
assumptions: State variables are taken as orthogonal axes
The mapping from state to location is unique
primitives.breakdown_regime: High-dimensional systems cannot be visualized directly; projections of the phase space can hide the structure that matters

layer2.mapping: Game scripts are read as regions of a state space (score differential by time remaining by field position); a team being 'in control' means its trajectory sits in a region where almost all continuations end one way.
layer2.telemetry: Historical trajectories of comparable games plotted in score-time-field-position space

primitives.name: For an iterative map, equilibrium points are states that stay unchanged over time, found by solving x_eq = F(x_eq)
primitives.verbatim_quote: one of the first things you should do is to find its equilibrium points (also called fixed points or steady states), i.e., states where the system can stay unchanged over time.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_{eq}: equilibrium state value, in the units of the state variable
symbol_and_unit_ledger.F: the one-step transition function of the iterative map

assumptions: The map is autonomous: F does not depend explicitly on time
The system is first-order: the next state depends on the current state only
primitives.breakdown_regime: Time-varying or higher-order systems need state augmentation before this fixed-point equation applies

layer2.mapping: Pregame ratings are treated as equilibrium claims: the level at which a unit's output stops drifting given its inputs; deviations from that level are the signal the reasoning layer must explain rather than average away.
layer2.telemetry: Rolling unit performance series tested for mean reversion toward a fitted equilibrium level

primitives.name: The discrete logistic growth model has exactly two equilibria: extinction at 0 and saturation at the carrying capacity K
primitives.verbatim_quote: The result shows that the population will not change if there are no organisms (xeq = 0) or if the population size reaches the carrying capacity of the environment (xeq = K).

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_t: population size at time step t, count of individuals
symbol_and_unit_ledger.r: intrinsic growth rate per time step, dimensionless

assumptions: Growth is proportional to current size and to the unused fraction of capacity
No migration, no age structure, constant r and K
primitives.breakdown_regime: With time-varying capacity or Allee effects the two-equilibrium picture fails; large r drives the map into oscillation and chaos instead of saturation

layer2.mapping: Usage and workload have carrying capacities: a player's touch share saturates against a team-level ceiling, so projections must bend growth curves toward the cap instead of extrapolating early-season rates linearly.
layer2.telemetry: Weekly touch/target shares per player against team play volume ceilings

primitives.name: Rescaling the logistic growth model yields the logistic map x_t = r x_{t-1} (1 - x_{t-1}), the most extensively studied one-dimensional nonlinear iterative map
primitives.verbatim_quote: has a designated name; it is called the logistic map. It is arguably the most extensively studied 1-D nonlinear iterative map.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_t: rescaled population at step t, dimensionless fraction of capacity

assumptions: Population rescaled by carrying capacity so K disappears
Single parameter r carries all qualitative dynamics
primitives.breakdown_regime: The map is a caricature: real populations have noise, structure, and multiple interacting species that one parameter cannot carry

layer2.mapping: One-parameter families warn the engine that a single driving rate (pace, pressure rate, blitz rate) can flip a unit's behavior qualitatively as it crosses thresholds, so parameter sweeps beat point estimates near regime boundaries.
layer2.telemetry: Unit performance as a function of a single swept driver, checked for threshold flips

primitives.name: Variable rescaling can eliminate as many parameters as the model has variables, and should be tried before mathematical analysis
primitives.verbatim_quote: You should try variable rescaling to eliminate as many parameters as possible from your model before conducting a mathematical analysis.
assumptions: Variables can be re-expressed in natural units of the problem
The rescaling is a pure change of units and changes no dynamics
primitives.breakdown_regime: Not every parameter is removable; parameters that encode genuinely independent mechanisms survive any rescaling

layer2.mapping: Ratings are nondimensionalized against league baselines before combination, which removes spurious scale parameters and keeps unlike signals (EPA, success rate, pressure rate) commensurable inside one reasoning pass.
layer2.telemetry: League-average baselines per metric per season used as rescaling units

primitives.name: Linear stability analysis rewrites dynamics around an equilibrium in terms of a small perturbation and drops higher-order terms
primitives.verbatim_quote: The basic idea of linear stability analysis is to rewrite the dynamics of the system in terms of a small perturbation added to the equilibrium point of your interest.
assumptions: Perturbations are infinitesimally small, so squared and higher terms are negligible
The equilibrium point itself is known exactly
primitives.breakdown_regime: Says nothing about behavior far from the equilibrium; large shocks, injuries, or scheme changes leave the regime where the linearization is valid

layer2.mapping: Injury and lineup news is priced as a perturbation test: a small change near a stable projection moves the estimate slightly, while the same change near an unstable one (a thin offensive line, a one-read offense) can flip it, and the reasoning layer must say which case applies.
layer2.telemetry: Projection sensitivity runs perturbing one input at a time around the pregame state

primitives.name: Stability of an equilibrium is decided by the Jacobian's eigenvalues at that point: dominant eigenvalue magnitude below 1 is stable, above 1 is unstable (discrete time)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Calculate the Jacobian matrix of the system at the equilibrium point.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\lambda_d: dominant eigenvalue of the Jacobian at the equilibrium, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.J: Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives of the transition function at the equilibrium

assumptions: The system is differentiable at the equilibrium
Discrete-time dynamics, where the unit circle is the stability boundary
primitives.breakdown_regime: Eigenvalue exactly at magnitude 1 is the marginal case the test cannot decide; non-smooth systems (thresholds, discrete plays) violate differentiability

layer2.mapping: Feedback loops in a matchup (a defense that must blitz more as it falls behind) are checked for amplification: if each loop multiplies a deviation by more than one, the projection should widen its uncertainty band instead of holding a point estimate.
layer2.telemetry: Estimated feedback gains between coupled unit metrics across a game script

primitives.name: For a continuous-time model dx/dt = G(x), equilibria solve 0 = G(x_eq) because a constant state makes the left hand side zero
primitives.verbatim_quote: This actually makes the left hand side zero, because xeq is no longer a dynamical variable but just a static constant.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.G: the vector field giving the rate of change of the state
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_{eq}: constant equilibrium state, in the units of the state variable

assumptions: The model is autonomous: G has no explicit time dependence
Equilibria are constant states, not cycles
primitives.breakdown_regime: Systems with periodic forcing have no constant equilibria; limit cycles require a different analysis

layer2.mapping: Continuous in-game win probability flow is anchored at states where the rates balance; the engine reads a stalled drive rate or a bleeding clock as movement toward or away from those balance points.
layer2.telemetry: Second-by-second game state with scoring-rate differentials

primitives.name: The Lotka-Volterra model describes predator-prey interactions, the canonical two-species coupled nonlinear system
primitives.verbatim_quote: The model we have created above is actually a variation of the Lotka-Volterra model, which describes various forms of predator-prey interactions.
assumptions: Prey grows logistically on its own; predators decay exponentially without prey
Encounters are proportional to the product of the two populations
primitives.breakdown_regime: No functional response saturation, no refuge, no third species; real coupled systems rarely stay on the neutral cycles of the basic model

layer2.mapping: Offense-defense pairs are coupled oscillators: a pass rush that feeds on obvious passing downs grows when the offense trails, and starves when the run game keeps downs short; projections must evolve the pair jointly, not rate each side in isolation.
layer2.telemetry: Down-by-down splits of pressure rate and play mix by score state

primitives.name: A bifurcation is a qualitative, topological change of a system's phase space when parameters cross critical thresholds
primitives.verbatim_quote: Bifurcation is a qualitative, topological change of a system’s phase space that occurs when some parameters are slightly varied across their critical thresholds.
assumptions: A parameter can be varied continuously across the threshold
The change is qualitative: the structure of trajectories changes, not just their speed
primitives.breakdown_regime: Noise can smear or trigger threshold crossings early; in finite real systems the sharp mathematical threshold becomes a transition zone

layer2.mapping: Threshold effects are first-class in the reasoning layer: a quarterback under a pressure rate above a critical band, or a defense losing its second corner, can change the kind of game being played, not just shift a projection by a point.
layer2.telemetry: Performance curves scanned for breakpoints as a driver (pressure, fatigue, score gap) varies

primitives.name: Period-doubling bifurcations cascade with geometrically shrinking intervals until the period diverges to infinity, which is the onset of chaos
primitives.verbatim_quote: Figure 8.10 showed a cascade of period-doubling bifurcations, with the intervals between consecutive bifurcation thresholds getting shorter and shorter geometrically as r increased.
assumptions: The system is a smooth one-parameter family of maps
Bifurcation intervals shrink by a roughly constant ratio
primitives.breakdown_regime: The cascade picture is exact for unimodal maps; multi-parameter or noisy systems can reach chaos by other routes (intermittency, torus breakdown)

layer2.mapping: Escalation dynamics (each answer forcing a faster answer, as in a shootout script) can pass through a few visible doublings of tempo before the game state becomes effectively unpredictable; the engine widens bands as escalation frequency rises.
layer2.telemetry: Drive tempo and scoring frequency series within games, watched for escalation patterns

primitives.name: Chaos is long-term behavior of a nonlinear dynamical system that never falls into static or periodic trajectories, deterministic yet effectively unpredictable
primitives.verbatim_quote: is a long-term behavior of a nonlinear dynamical system that never falls in any static or periodic trajectories.
assumptions: The system is nonlinear and deterministic
The trajectory is bounded but never repeats periodically
primitives.breakdown_regime: Chaos is not randomness: stochastic systems are a different category, and short-term prediction in chaotic systems still works

layer2.mapping: Some game states are chaotic in this precise sense: deterministic play-by-play rules but no stable script, where the honest output is a distribution over outcomes with a short prediction horizon, not a confident single line.
layer2.telemetry: Forecast skill decay measured as a function of horizon for volatile matchup classes

primitives.name: The Lyapunov exponent is the time average of log |dF/dx| along the trajectory and measures how fast nearby states separate
primitives.verbatim_quote: The final result is quite simple—the Lyapunov exponent is a time average of log |dF/dx| at every state the system visits over the course of the simulation.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\lambda: Lyapunov exponent, per time step; positive values mean exponential separation of nearby trajectories
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_i: the state visited at step i

assumptions: The trajectory is long enough for the time average to converge
The map is differentiable along the visited states
primitives.breakdown_regime: Finite data gives only an estimate; a positive exponent in a noisy fitted model may reflect noise rather than deterministic chaos

layer2.mapping: Forecast divergence is quantified, not vibes: the engine can measure how fast two nearly identical pregame states (one player questionable versus active) separate in projected outcomes, and cap its confidence at the measured divergence rate.
layer2.telemetry: Paired projection runs from perturbed initial states, logging outcome separation over game time

primitives.name: Cellular automata are automata on a regular spatial grid, simultaneously updated by a uniform state-transition function of their neighbors' states
primitives.verbatim_quote: Cellular automata (CA) [18] are a set of such automata arranged along a regular spatial grid, whose states are simultaneously updated by a uniformly applied state-transition function that refers to the states of their neighbors.
assumptions: Space and states are discrete; the grid is regular
The same transition function and neighborhood apply everywhere (spatial homogeneity)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Real spatial systems are rarely homogeneous or regular; network models exist precisely to relax this assumption

layer2.mapping: Field-level processes (pressure spreading along an offensive line, coverage rotations propagating) can be simulated as local update rules on a grid, giving the engine a cheap way to generate emergent line-level behavior from per-player rules.
layer2.telemetry: Per-position unit states on a formation grid updated snap by snap

primitives.name: The CA update rule computes each cell's next state from the current states of its fixed neighborhood
primitives.verbatim_quote: where st (x) is the state of an automaton located at x at time t, F is the state-transition function, and N = {x0 , x1 , . . . , xn−1 } is the neighborhood.
primitives.latex: s_{t+1}(x) = F\big(s_t(x + x_0), s_t(x + x_1), \ldots, s_t(x + x_{n-1})\big)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.s_t(x): state of the cell at position x at time t, discrete state label
symbol_and_unit_ledger.F: state-transition function, identical for all cells
symbol_and_unit_ledger.N: the neighborhood offset set, in grid units

assumptions: Updating is synchronous across all cells
Interactions are strictly local within the neighborhood
primitives.breakdown_regime: Asynchronous updating or long-range interactions break the classical CA form and can change the resulting patterns

layer2.mapping: Local interaction kernels are the template for matchup simulation: a receiver's separation on a snap is computed from his own state and his immediate neighbors (the covering defender, the safety's position), then aggregated, rather than assigned from a global rating.
layer2.telemetry: Snap-level neighbor states: nearest defender distance, help position, leverage

primitives.name: In the epidemic/forest fire CA, a tree catches fire if at least one neighbor burns, and a burning tree is charred after one step: a minimal threshold contact process
primitives.verbatim_quote: A tree will catch fire if there is at least one tree burning in its neighborhood, and the burning tree will be charred (3) completely after one time step.
assumptions: Trees are placed independently with probability p
Spread is to immediate neighbors only, one step per generation
primitives.breakdown_regime: Real contagion has heterogeneous susceptibility and long-range jumps; the single-neighbor threshold understates superspreading

layer2.mapping: Contagion processes inside a team (an injury cluster at one position group, a coverage bust pattern spreading across a secondary) follow threshold contact dynamics: one failure raises the failure probability of adjacent units on the next snap.
layer2.telemetry: Positional adjacency of failures: busts, penalties, and missed assignments by neighboring positions over consecutive snaps

primitives.name: The diffusion equation dc/dt = alpha Laplacian c + s is the fundamental PDE for spreading driven by local random motion
primitives.verbatim_quote: Now we see the Laplacian coming out! This is called the diffusion equation, one of the most fundamental PDEs that has been applied to many spatio-temporal dynamics in physics, biology, ecology, engineering, social science, marketing science, and many other disciplines.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.c: concentration or density of the spreading quantity, per unit area or volume
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\alpha: diffusion constant, area per unit time
symbol_and_unit_ledger.s: source term, quantity per unit area per unit time

assumptions: Movement is unbiased random walk at the micro level
The continuum limit applies: many particles, small steps
primitives.breakdown_regime: Directed transport (advection, chemotaxis) and long jumps violate pure diffusion and need extra terms

layer2.mapping: Yardage and field position diffuse: a drive's field position spreads from its start with a rate set by play mix, and the diffusion constant per team is a measurable style parameter the engine can estimate from drive histories.
layer2.telemetry: Drive start and end field positions across a season, fitted as a diffusion process

primitives.name: Reaction-diffusion systems couple local reaction terms R_i with pure Laplacian diffusion terms D_i, and nothing else spatial
primitives.verbatim_quote: Reaction terms (Ri (. . .)) describe only local dynamics, without any spatial derivatives involved. Diffusion terms (Di ∇2 fi ) are strictly limited to the Laplacian of the state variable itself.
primitives.latex: \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t} = R_i(f_1, \ldots, f_n) + D_i \nabla^2 f_i

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_i: concentration of component i, per unit area
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R_i: local reaction rate for component i, per unit time
symbol_and_unit_ledger.D_i: diffusion constant of component i, area per unit time

assumptions: Spatial coupling is diffusion only, no advection or chemotaxis
Reactions are purely local functions of the component concentrations
primitives.breakdown_regime: When components move at very different speeds pattern formation appears; when a component is actively transported the system leaves the reaction-diffusion class

layer2.mapping: Pattern formation logic maps to scheme emergence: local rules (a coverage's reaction to a route concept) plus spatial spreading (adjustments propagating across the field) can generate stable patterns, like a defense's recurring bust against one formation, that no single play call explains.
layer2.telemetry: Formation-by-formation defensive bust rates and their spread across a game

primitives.name: A network's degree distribution P(k) is the probability that a node has degree k, the fraction of nodes with exactly k connections
primitives.verbatim_quote: A degree distribution of a network is a probability distribution

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(k): probability a randomly chosen node has degree k, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.deg(i): degree of node i, count of edges

assumptions: The network is a static snapshot for the measurement
Degree counts edges without weights unless a weighted variant is defined
primitives.breakdown_regime: A single snapshot distribution hides temporal rewiring; directed networks need separate in- and out-degree distributions

layer2.mapping: Target and touch distributions are degree distributions: the shape (hub-dominated versus flat) tells the reasoning layer whether an offense runs through one node whose removal collapses the structure or through a flat rotation that absorbs losses.
layer2.telemetry: Per-player target, carry, and snap-share histograms per team per week

primitives.name: The clustering coefficient of a node is the probability that its neighbors are also neighbors of each other
primitives.verbatim_quote: Therefore, the clustering coefficient of node i calculates the probability for its neighbors to be each other’s neighbors as well.
assumptions: The network is undirected for this metric
The node has at least two neighbors, or the coefficient is undefined
primitives.breakdown_regime: Undefined or misleading for very low-degree nodes; weighted and directed variants give different values

layer2.mapping: Clustering measures redundancy in a passing network: if a quarterback's top targets also connect heavily to each other (shared routes, same side of the field), removing one target reroutes less cleanly than the raw share suggests.
layer2.telemetry: Co-targeting matrices: how often pairs of receivers are targeted on the same drives and formations

primitives.name: Watts-Strogatz small-world networks combine very high clustering with short paths, unlike their random counterparts
primitives.verbatim_quote: The clustering coefficient was first introduced by Watts and Strogatz [56], where they showed that their small-world networks tend to have very high clustering compared to their random counterparts.
assumptions: Comparison is against a random network of comparable size and density
A small rewiring probability interpolates between a regular lattice and a random graph
primitives.breakdown_regime: High clustering alone is not small-world; the short average path length must also be verified

layer2.mapping: Schedule and matchup graphs are small-world: most opponents cluster inside divisions, but a few long-range edges (cross-conference games) carry outsized information about true team strength, and the reasoning layer should weight those bridge games heavily.
layer2.telemetry: Season schedule graph with clustering by division and the bridge games between clusters

primitives.name: In the Barabasi-Albert model a newcomer connects to existing node i with probability proportional to its degree, p(i) = deg(i) / sum_j deg(j)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Here p(i) is the probability for an existing node i to be connected by a newcomer node, which is proportional to its degree (preferential attachment).

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p(i): probability that a new edge attaches to node i, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.deg(i): current degree of node i, count of edges

assumptions: The network grows one node at a time
Attachment probability is exactly linear in current degree
primitives.breakdown_regime: Sublinear or superlinear attachment changes the degree distribution away from a pure power law; aging and fitness effects break pure degree proportionality

layer2.mapping: Usage concentration is a preferential attachment process: targets breed targets because coverage rolls toward the hot receiver slowly while the quarterback's trust compounds; the engine projects share growth with an attachment kernel instead of freezing early-season shares.
layer2.telemetry: Week-over-week target share changes regressed on current share to estimate the attachment exponent

primitives.name: Networks whose degree distributions follow a power law P(k) ~ k^-gamma are scale-free, with hub nodes that a normal distribution would forbid
primitives.verbatim_quote: Barabási and Albert called networks whose degree distributions follow a power law scale-free networks, because there is no characteristic “scale” that stands out in their degree distributions.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.P(k): probability a node has degree k, dimensionless
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\gamma: scaling exponent; gamma = 3 in the Barabasi-Albert model

assumptions: The power law holds over a broad range of k, not just the tail
The network is large enough for the tail to be populated
primitives.breakdown_regime: Finite networks always truncate the tail; many claimed power laws fail rigorous fitting against log-normal alternatives

layer2.mapping: Player production is heavy-tailed: a few hub players carry a disproportionate share of team output, so the reasoning layer prices the loss of a hub as a structural change, while the loss of a median node is a rounding adjustment.
layer2.telemetry: Distribution of team EPA share across players, fitted for tail heaviness per team

primitives.name: The Kuramoto model couples phase oscillators through the sine of their phase differences, with coupling strength alpha, and produces collective synchronization
primitives.verbatim_quote: To represent this type of phase-based interaction among coupled oscillators, a Japanese physicist Yoshiki Kuramoto proposed the following very simple, elegant mathematical model in the 1970s [70]:

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\omega_i: natural frequency of oscillator i, radians per unit time

assumptions: Interactions depend only on phase differences through a sine coupling
Each oscillator has a fixed natural frequency
primitives.breakdown_regime: Below a critical coupling the population stays incoherent; strongly heterogeneous frequencies or adversarial coupling prevent synchronization

layer2.mapping: Unit cohesion is synchronization: an offensive line's five blockers are oscillators whose timing either locks (combo blocks arriving together) or drifts (stunts exploiting the gaps), and the lock quality is a measurable state variable, not a chemistry narrative.
layer2.telemetry: Timing dispersion of coordinated actions: line get-off times, route break synchronization, snap-to-throw rhythm

primitives.name: Phase coherence is an order parameter that equals 1 when all nodes are perfectly synchronized and 0 when phases are completely random
primitives.verbatim_quote: This measurement becomes 1 if all the nodes are in perfect synchronization, or 0 if their phases are completely random and uniformly distributed in the angular space.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.r: phase coherence order parameter, dimensionless between 0 and 1

assumptions: Phases live on a circle and are averaged as unit vectors
All nodes weighted equally
primitives.breakdown_regime: The scalar hides cluster structure: two opposed synchronized clusters can average to a deceptively low or high value depending on sizes

layer2.mapping: A single coherence number per unit per game (line timing, secondary communication, route timing) gives the reasoning layer a comparable, trackable cohesion signal across weeks instead of prose impressions.
layer2.telemetry: Per-game coherence scores computed from timing dispersion of coordinated unit actions

primitives.name: In adaptive networks, node state transitions and topological transformations are deeply coupled, producing state-topology co-evolution
primitives.verbatim_quote: In these adaptive networks, state transitions of each node and topological transformation of networks are deeply coupled with each other, which could produce characteristic behaviors that are not found in other forms of dynamical network models.
assumptions: Both node states and the edge structure evolve in time
Each dynamics runs on a timescale that can influence the other
primitives.breakdown_regime: If topology changes much faster or slower than states, the coupling effectively decouples and static-network or mean-field methods suffice

layer2.mapping: A team's target network rewires as it plays: injuries and coverage responses change both player states and the connection structure, so the engine updates the network and the node values together after every game instead of re-rating players on a fixed graph.
layer2.telemetry: Weekly target and personnel networks with node performance states, tracked as joint evolution

primitives.name: Agent-based models are computational simulation models that involve many discrete agents
primitives.verbatim_quote: Agent-based models are computational simulation models that involve many discrete agents.
assumptions: Agents are discrete entities with their own behavioral rules
The model is run as a simulation rather than solved in closed form
primitives.breakdown_regime: With no constraints on agent rules, an ABM can fit anything post hoc; explanatory value requires the rules to be stated before outcomes are inspected

layer2.mapping: The pre-simulation layer is an ABM in this sense: players as agents with stated behavioral rules (route choices, rush moves, coverage responsibilities) generate the matchup behavior that the analytic layers then summarize.
layer2.telemetry: Agent rule sets per position with parameters fitted from tracking and play data

primitives.name: ABMs are the most generalized modeling framework in the book: cellular automata and dynamical networks are special cases of them
primitives.verbatim_quote: ABMs are arguably the most generalized framework for modeling and simulation of complex systems, which actually include both cellular automata and dynamical networks as special cases.
assumptions: CA are recovered when agents sit on a regular grid with uniform rules
Dynamical networks are recovered when agents sit on a fixed or evolving graph
primitives.breakdown_regime: Generality is not accuracy: the special-case frameworks often admit analysis that the general ABM does not

layer2.mapping: Framework choice is a ladder: use the most restrictive model that still expresses the mechanism (map, CA, network, full ABM), because restrictiveness is what makes a projection falsifiable; the reasoning trail names the rung used.
layer2.telemetry: Model registry tagging each projection with the framework rung it was produced on

primitives.name: Schelling's model shows segregation emerges at a much lower homophily threshold than intuition expects, and very high homophily can paradoxically produce a mixed state
primitives.verbatim_quote: But what Schelling actually showed was that the critical threshold can be much lower than one would expect. This means that segregation can occur even if people aren’t so homophilic.
assumptions: Agents move when the same-type fraction among neighbors falls below their threshold
Agents choose new locations at random in a finite two-dimensional space

reasoning_traces.think: This book is a complete operating system for thinking about systems whose behavior is generated by interacting parts, and its machinery assembles in a deliberate order. It begins with a philosophy: a model is a simplified representation, science is the endless construction of such representations, and two cross-cutting phenomena, emergence and self-organization, are what make the representations nontrivial. Emergence says the macroscopic property is not a simple sum of microscopic ones. Self-organization says the macroscopic order can arise over time from the interactions themselves, in an open system, without a controller. Everything after Chapter 1 is a sequence of increasingly expressive ways to write down the microscopic rules and then read off the macroscopic consequences. The dynamical systems chapters supply the grammar: a state, a set of variables that uniquely specifies it, a phase space in which every state is a location, and rules that move the state through that space. Once that grammar exists, the first analytic questions are always the same. Where are the equilibrium points, the states that reproduce themselves? Are they stable, meaning does a small perturbation decay or grow? The discrete-time chapters answer with fixed-point equations and with linearization: rewrite the dynamics around the equilibrium in terms of a small perturbation, build the Jacobian, and let the eigenvalues vote. The logistic family is the laboratory for all of this. The logistic growth model has two transparent equilibria, extinction and carrying capacity. Rescaling strips it to the logistic map, one parameter, and that one parameter turns out to contain period doubling, a cascade whose intervals shrink geometrically, and then chaos: deterministic behavior with no period at all, whose unpredictability is measured rather than asserted, through the Lyapunov exponent as a time average of log derivative magnitudes along the trajectory. The continuous-time chapters mirror the discrete ones, with equilibria solving G(x) equal to zero and coupled systems like Lotka-Volterra showing how two species, or any two coupled quantities, oscillate because each one's growth rate is the other one's state. Bifurcation theory names the moment the whole picture changes: a parameter crosses a critical threshold and the phase space itself is topologically rearranged, so the analyst's job is not only to locate equilibria but to map the thresholds at which the equilibrium structure is replaced. Part III then scales the number of components. Cellular automata put identical dynamical variables on a grid and let a uniform local rule generate global pattern, including threshold contact processes like the epidemic and forest fire model where one burning neighbor is enough to propagate the front. Continuous field models replace the grid with partial differential equations: diffusion spreads quantities with the Laplacian, and reaction-diffusion systems show that local reactions plus pure diffusion are already sufficient for pattern formation. Network models relax the grid's regularity. The static analysis contributes the descriptive statistics: degree distributions, which in growing networks with preferential attachment become power laws with hubs, and clustering coefficients, which with short path lengths define the small-world regime. The dynamic chapters then let the network itself move: Kuramoto oscillators synchronize through sine coupling when the coupling is strong enough, with phase coherence as a clean order parameter between zero and one, and adaptive networks close the loop by letting node states and topology change each other. Agent-based models sit at the top of the ladder as the most general framework, with cellular automata and dynamical networks as special cases, and Schelling's segregation model as the standing warning that strong macroscopic pattern can emerge from thresholds far weaker than intuition demands. For a reasoning engine, the value of this machinery is discipline. It forces every claim into one of a few shapes: an equilibrium claim, a stability claim, a threshold claim, a distribution-shape claim, a synchronization claim, or an emergence claim, and each shape carries its own test. A projection that says a unit will keep performing at its current level is an equilibrium claim and must survive a perturbation test. A projection that says a matchup flips if one player is removed is a bifurcation claim and must name the threshold. A projection built on one star is a hub claim and must price the heavy tail. Two further habits deserve extraction because they transfer directly. The first is rescaling before analysis: the logistic growth model carries two parameters until a change of units reveals that only one combination of them matters, and the same discipline applied to any rating system removes dimensions that were never real degrees of freedom. Fewer effective parameters means fewer ways to overfit and a cleaner map of where the thresholds actually sit. The second habit is the paired presentation of simulation and analysis. Simulation shows what a rule does; analysis shows why, and where it must stop doing it. A simulation without analysis can be a coincidence with good graphics. An analysis without simulation can be a proof about a regime the system never visits. The book refuses to publish either one alone, and an engine should hold itself to the same refusal. The network chapters add one more transferable warning about measurement. A degree distribution is a claim about shape, and shape claims are falsifiable in a way that average claims are not: two networks with the same average degree can be a homogeneous mesh or a hub system, and they fail in completely different ways when a node is removed. Any aggregate that reports only the mean of a distribution whose shape drives the behavior is hiding the load-bearing information. The book also supplies the failure vocabulary. Linearization fails far from equilibrium. Fixed rules fail when the agents adapt. Homogeneous grids fail when the real connection structure is a network. A model that cannot state which of these failures it is exposed to has not finished its work. That is the standard this extraction encodes: every primitive is either a definition that fixes language, an equation that fixes computation, or a named regime change that fixes where the computation stops being valid.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from von Neumann and Ulam inventing cellular automata in the 1940s and 1950s to model self-reproduction, through Lorenz and the discovery of chaos in deterministic systems, May's work on the logistic map in ecology, Watts and Strogatz on small worlds in 1998, Barabasi and Albert on preferential attachment in 1999, and Kuramoto's 1970s synchronization model imported from physics. Sayama's genealogy is explicit that complex systems science is a confluence: nonlinear dynamics, systems theory, and game theory as historical roots, with pattern formation, evolution and adaptation, networks, and collective behavior as the newer topical clusters that grew once computation became cheap enough to simulate what analysis could not solve.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Sayama's model of the reader is a working scientist in training: someone who should never mistake the model for the reality, who should rescale before analyzing, find equilibria before simulating, and treat simulation and analysis as two views of the same object, which is why most topics get paired computational and mathematical chapters. His model of the domain is that cross-disciplinary generality is real: the same logistic map governs a population and a learning curve because the mechanism, growth limited by saturation, is shared. He trusts simple rules honestly explored over elaborate models weakly understood, and he expects the reader to verify every claim by running the code.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in this book veto common reasoning shortcuts. The chaos chapters veto long-horizon point prediction in sensitive regimes: when the Lyapunov exponent is positive, confidence must decay at a measured rate, and any layer that outputs a single confident number far downstream is overruled. The bifurcation material vetoes linear extrapolation across thresholds: near a critical parameter value, small input changes are not small output changes. Schelling vetoes intent attribution from pattern: a clustered outcome does not prove a strong preference or a deliberate scheme. And the linearization chapters veto stability claims made far from equilibrium: a perturbation analysis is only licensed near the point it was computed at.

universal_lens: Read as a general template, this book says: any system of many interacting parts can be approached with the same sequence. Fix the state variables. Write the local rules. Find the equilibria and test their stability. Map the thresholds where the structure changes. Measure the distribution shapes and the coupling structure. Only then simulate the general case. The sequence is domain-free: it applies to ecosystems, economies, epidemics, organizations, and software systems with equal force, because the questions are about dynamics, not about subject matter.
gsi_mapping: The Galaxy Sports Institute takes the book as curriculum and as method. As curriculum, it is the single-volume spine for teaching modeling: dynamical systems, bifurcations, chaos, cellular automata, fields, networks, and agent-based models in one consistent notation with runnable code. As method, it supplies the audit questions for any submitted model: What is the state? Where are the equilibria? What is the stability argument? Where are the thresholds? What distribution shape is assumed, and was it measured? A submission that cannot answer is returned, whatever its headline accuracy.
gse_mapping: The Galaxy Sports Edge engine takes five concrete mechanisms. Equilibrium and stability analysis turns ratings into testable fixed-point claims with perturbation pricing for injuries and lineup news. Bifurcation mapping names the thresholds where a matchup changes kind rather than degree. Power-law degree structure prices hub players as structural single points of failure. Synchronization and phase coherence turn unit cohesion into a measurable weekly signal. And the Lyapunov discipline caps forecast confidence by measured divergence rates, so the reasoning trail states not only a projection but the horizon over which that projection deserves trust.
